*Geschlecht*de{}|Alternative forms}Geschlächt|Etymology}From Middle High German geslechte,from Old High German gislahti,a collective formation from Old High German slahta,from Proto-Germanic ⋆slahtō,related to from Proto-Germanic tto strike,hit (DWDS).}Cognate with from Dutch geslacht,from Middle Low German geslechte,from Italian schiatta,from Polish szlachta. The Germanic root is that of Schlag,schlagen. The modern sense developed among this root's descendants first in Menschenschlag,in which the underlying meaning of ''Schlag'' is "strike of coinage".|Pronunciation}IPA:/ɡəˈʃlɛçt/}Ⓓ6/64/De-Geschlecht.ogg}Rhymes:ɛçt|Noun}(neut.,genitive:Geschlechtses,plural:[Geschlechtereobsolete])}#sex}#grammar gender}#}Geschlecht Die Deutsche Sprache ordnet,wie jede andere,ihre Substantive nach gewissen '''Geschlechtern''',deren wir drei haben:1) das männliche (masculinum),2) das weibliche (femininum),3) das sächliche (neutrum). Kommen die beiden ersten '''Geschlechter''' einem Worte zugleich zu,so sagt man:sein '''Geschlecht''' ist ein Doppelgeschlecht oder ein gemeinschaftliches (commune); kommen ihm alle drei zu,so ist es generis omnis,oder ein Allgeschlecht.}:translationLike every other language,German orders its nouns into certain '''genders''',of which we have three:1) the masculine (masculinum),2) the feminine (femininum),3) the neuter (neutrum). Where both of the first two '''genders''' apply equally to a word,its '''gender''' is called a double-gender or a common (commune); where all three apply,it is called generis omnis,or an all-gender.}#sex organ}#genus,type,race}#lineage,generation,family}#dynasty,house|Synonyms}sense:grammatical gender Genus,Wortgeschlecht}sense:genital organ Genital,Geschlechtsorgan,Geschlechtsteil}sense:genus Gattung,Genus}sense:dynasty Dynastie,Haus|Hyponyms}Adelsgeschlecht}Menschengeschlecht}Naturgeschlecht}Sachgeschlecht}Sprachgeschlecht}Wortgeschlecht|Derived terms}geschlechtlich}eingeschlechtig

*gewohnt*de{}|Etymology}Compare cog:wont.|Pronunciation}IPA:ɡəˈvoːnt}De-at-gewohnt.ogg(Austria)}Ⓓ0/0b/De-gewohnt.ogg}ge+wohnt|Participle}gewohnt:}#past participle of [wohnen]|Adjective}#usual,customary,familiar}#used to,wont,familiar gewohnt ( with  acc/genarchaicto/with something)|Usage notes}The phrases  and  have very similar meanings and can often be used more or less interchangeably. However,they have different constructions. The former is construed with direct accusative or zu+infinitive,the latter with an+accusative:}Dieses heiße Wetter bin ich nicht '''gewohnt'''.}•I’m not '''used to''' this hot weather.}An dieses heiße Wetter bin ich nicht '''gewöhnt'''.}•I’m not '''accustomed''' to this hot weather.}Ich bin '''gewohnt''',früh aufzustehen.}•I’m '''used to''' getting up early.}Ich bin daran '''gewöhnt''',früh aufzustehen.}•I’m '''accustomed''' to getting up early.}A totally different matter is the use of  and  with the perfect auxiliary haben. In this case,is the participle of wohnen:}Viele Jahre hatte ich in Berlin '''gewohnt'''.}•For many years I had '''lived''' in Berlin.}Nur langsam hatte ich mich an das Leben dort '''gewöhnt'''.}•Only slowly had I '''got accustomed''' to life there.|Derived terms}gewohntermaßen}ungewohnt

*gleich*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German gelīch,from Old High German gilīh,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆galīk,from Proto-Germanic ⋆galīkaz. Cognate with from Dutch gelijk,from English alike,from Swedish lik,from Danish lig.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ɡlaɪ̯ç/}Ⓓ7/7f/De-gleich.ogg}Rhymes:aɪ̯ç|Adjective}#equal}•Zwei plus zwei ist '''gleich''' vier.}•Two plus two is '''equal''' to four.}#same; very similar}•Zufälligerweise hatten wir beide die '''gleiche''' Idee.}•Coincidentally,we both had the '''same''' idea.}#often proscribed same; identical|Usage notes}See derselbe for notes on the prescribed distinction between this word and gleich.}The comparative forms are rather rare. They occur chiefly in colloquial or informal usage; for example:Diese beiden Socken sind ziemlich gleich,aber die anderen beiden sind noch '''gleicher'''. (“These two socks are pretty identical,but those other two are even more identical.”) There is also a common humorous saying that goes:Im Kommunismus waren alle gleich. Aber manche waren '''gleicher'''. (“Everyone was equal in communism. But some were more equal than the others.”)|Adverb}#alike}•Er malt alle seine Bilder '''gleich'''.}•He paints all of his pictures '''alike'''.}#in a moment}•Warte,ich komme '''gleich''' zu dir.}•Hold on,I'll come to you '''in a moment'''.}#at once,at a time,simultaneously}•Weil ich hungrig war,habe ich mir '''gleich''' zwei Stücke Kuchen vom Buffet genommen.}•Because I was hungry,I took two pieces of cake '''at once''' from the buffet.}#}gleich Entdeckung im All:'''Gleich''' zwei erdähnliche Planeten kreisen um den Zwergstern Gliese 581.}•Discovery in the universe:two Earth-like planets at once revolve around the dwarf star Gliese 581.}#right; just; directly}•Mein Haus befindet '''gleich''' neben dem Stadtpark.}•My house is located '''right''' next to the city park.}#now; immediately; straight away}•Nachdem sie im Hotel angekommen war,legte sie sich '''gleich''' ins Bett.}•After she had arrived at the hotel,she '''immediately''' went to bed.|Derived terms}abgleichen}angleichen}gegengleich}gleichen}gleichfalls}gleichermaßen}gleichgültig}Gleichheit}Gleichstand}Gleichung}gleichsam}gleichtun}gleichstellen}gleichzeitig}gleichwohl}immer gleich}Ausgleich}obgleich}ungleich}vergleichen}wenngleich}zeitgleich}zugleich}Pennsylvania German|Etymology}Compare from German gleich,from Dutch gelijk,from English like.|Adjective}gleich:}#equal}#like}#same

*Goodwill*de{}|Etymology}English goodwill|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Goodwill(s).sg])}#goodwill all senses}#}Goodwill Ist die Rückgewähr in natura möglich,sind wiederum keinesfalls die Grundsätze heranzuziehen,welche zum Nutzungsersatz bei Unternehmen diskutiert werden,die im Wege eines asset deals erworben wurden. Zwar werden für die Zwecke der Gewährleistung im Kaufrecht die beiden Arten des Unternehmenskaufs oftmals gleich gestellt. Doch im Rahmen des Rücktrittsrechts kann dies nicht gelten. Vielmehr ist dort das Trennungsprinzip zu wahren. Es geht daher nicht um die Nutzungen aus dem (und Verwendungen auf das) Unternehmen als Inbegriff von Sachen und Rechten einschließlich des '''Goodwill''',sondern um die Nutzungen aus Anteilen.

*Graupel*de{}|Etymology}16th century. From Graupe+-el+t1hulled grain+pos2diminutive suffix.  is from German ,where the senses “hulled grain” and “hail” are both present. Compare from Polish krupa,from Czech kroupa,from Serbo-Croatian krupa.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈɡʁaʊ̯pəl/}Ⓓ8/8b/De-Graupel.ogg}Grau+pel|Noun}(fem.) ''or''}msometimes informally)}#meteorology graupel; soft hail}•synononym Griesel|Usage notes}The word was originally a feminine referring to a single flake of graupel and hence chiefly used in the plural . *gucken*de{}|Alternative forms}reflecting the common pronunciation,but less frequent in writing|Etymology}From Middle High German gücken,from Middle High German tto look inquisitively,peek,peer,of from German nocap1 origin. Perhaps from a specialised use of from Middle High German gücken,from Middle High German tto cuckoo,call or cry like a cuckoo,from Old High German guckōn,from Old High German tto cuckoo. The pronunciation (and spelling) with ''k-'' is commonly explained as an influence of from German Low German kieken (from Middle Low German kîken). Note,however,that this pronunciation reaches far to the south (compare from Luxembourgish kucken and from Dutch kijken).|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈkʊkən/qualifier:commonly,northern}IPA:/ˈɡʊkən/qualifier:standard,southern}Ⓓ1/1d/De-gucken.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#colloquial to look,to direct one's gaze at something}•synononym [[[[schauen],[sehen]],[hinsehen]],[betrachten]],[ansehen]}#}gucken Ich kann in die Stadt gehen und mich irgendwo hinsetzen und in die Luft '''gucken'''.}•I can go into town and sit myself down somewhere and stare into space.}#colloquial to watch,to direct one's gaze at something for some time}#copulative to look,to have a certain facial expression}•synononym aussehen}•Warum '''guckst''' du so traurig?}•Why are you '''looking''' so sad?|Usage notes}''Gucken'',along with its spelling variant kucken,is the common word for "to look" in northern and central Germany. Southern German and Austrian varieties use schauen. ''Gucken'' is not normally used in formal language,where it is replaced with synonyms.|Derived terms}angucken}begucken}Guckloch}hergucken}hingucken}hinterhergucken}mitgucken}nachgucken}umgucken}zugucken

*H*de{}|Pronunciation}phoneme IPA:/h/}The letter is silent in the syllable coda,before IPAchar:/ə/,and before suffixes. In common speech,''h'' is frequently silent in the onset of all word-internal unstressed syllables,thus e.g. in -heit and -haft (unless these have secondary stress).}name IPA:/haː/}Ⓓ6/65/Ⓓ6/65/De-h.ogg}Rhymes:aː|Letter}H:}#The eighth letter of the German alphabet.|Usage notes}-top}Spelling rules for silent ''h''}For the use of silent ''h'' in German orthography one may note three general rules:}#It occurs only after long monophthongs and the diphthong ''ei''.}#It occurs after simple ''i'' only in the pronominal stems ihm,ihn,ihr,and in Schlemihl.}#It is mostly restricted to native Germanic words; instances in loanwords are exceptional.}Expanding on this,one can distinguish three types of silent ''h'':}#Etymological ''h'' is written in words where noncog:- had a consonant that has become silent; this was usually ''h'',occasionally ''g'' or ''w''. Etymological ''h'' is missing only in a few words (e.g. rau,Ton,Träne).}#Hiatus-breaking ''h'' is written when an inflectable word stem ends in a long monophthong. This,too,is missing only in a few native words (e.g. säen,certain nouns like Knie,See,Schnee).}#Lengthening ''h'' (in the strict sense) may be written between long ''a,ä,e,o,ö,u,ü'' and following ''l,m,n,r''. Its use is very irregular and it is missing in a great deal of words. At times this is done to distinguish homophones (e.g. malen vs. mahlen),but in general there is no clear system. One can note that lengthening ''h'' proper does not occur in stems starting with ''sch-,sp-,t-''. It is overall rare in words starting with more than one consonant,but there are several counterexamples (e.g. Drohne,prahlen,Stuhl).}-bottom|See also}list:Latin script letters/de|Pronunciation}IPA:/haː/}Ⓓ6/65/Ⓓ6/65/De-h.ogg}Rhymes:aː|Noun}(neut.,plural:[H.sg])}#music B|See also}B

However in German,unlike English,it is more common to use the plural:''Sie hat graue Haare.'' *Halve Hahn*de{}|Etymology}Borrowed ksh. The origin is possibly an order like Can I get half a sandwich?,the last two words of which were then re-interpreted (either by foreigners or jokingly) as ''halve Hahn''.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˌhalvəˈhaːn/|Noun}Halve Hahn:}#regional a cheese sandwich,cut in half|Usage notes}The expression is rare in actual usage. Even in thick Ripuarian dialect one generally uses the plain and simple word m:Kiesbrütche ("cheese sandwich"). However,''Halve Hahn'' is occasionally used as a shibboleth among Rhineland people and can be found on the menus of traditional Colognian pubs (as a humorous knowledge test for foreigners).}The term is either uninflected,e.g. (accusative) ''den Halve Hahn'',or the first part behaves like a normal German adjective,thus ''den Halve'''n''' Hahn'',and so on.

*handeln*de{}|Etymology 1}From Middle High German handeln,from Old High German hantalōn,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆handulōn.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈhandl̩n}Ⓓ0/03/De-handeln.ogg}han+deln|Verb}de-verb}#intransitive to act; to bargain; to haggle}•Da lass ich nicht mit mir '''handeln'''.}•I won’t '''bargain''' about this.}#intransitive to trade in; to deal; to sell handeln ( with  :mit(dat))}•Er '''handelt''' mit Teppichen.}•He '''trades''' in carpets.}#transitive to trade}•Eine Aktiengesellschaft ist eine Firma,die an der Börse '''gehandelt''' wird.}•A stock company is an enterprise that is '''traded''' in the stock market.}#}handeln In Toronto '''werden''' mehr als 1400 Bergbaubetriebe '''gehandelt''',jede Woche kommen im Schnitt drei Unternehmen hinzu.}•More than 1400 mining companies are traded in Toronto,three companies are added each week on average.}#transitive to tip as; to take into consideration as being}•Er wird als der nächste Superstar '''gehandelt'''.}•He’s being '''tipped''' as the next superstar.}#intransitive to discuss; to deal with; to write or speak about handeln ( with  :von)}•Der Autor '''handelt''' auf 32 Seiten von dieser Nebensächlichkeit.}•The author '''discusses''' this marginal issue in 32 pages.}#|of a text,film,etc. to be about; to deal with}•Das Buch '''handelt''' von Hasen.}•The book '''is''' about hares.}#impersonal to be,to be a case of,to be a matter of,to concern often used to introduce the subject before giving it a name,or to indicate some uncertainty regarding exact amounts qlit:it itself has to do with ... handeln ( with  :um(acc)something+:bei(dat)with respect to something else)}•Es '''handelt''' sich um ein Missverständnis.}•What we have '''is''' a misunderstanding.}•Bei diesen Tieren '''handelt''' es sich um Hasen.}•These animals here '''are''' hares.}•Es '''handelt''' sich um ein paar Tage,bis die Pakete ankommen werden.}•It will '''be''' a matter of days before the packages will arrive.|Derived terms}abhandeln}aushandeln}ausverhandeln}behandeln}einhandeln}erhandeln}gehandelt}Handeln}handelnd}Händler}Handlung}herunterhandeln}kuhhandeln}misshandeln}unterhandeln}verhandeln}zuwiderhandeln|See also}dealen|Etymology 2}Borrowed en. id1act.|Alternative forms}händeln|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhɛnd(ə)ln/|Verb}de-verb}#transitive to handle something; *handhabe*de{}|Pronunciation}Ⓓb/ba/De-handhabe.ogg|Verb}#verb form of [handhaben]
*handhaben*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German hanthaben (1349). The earliest sense is “to keep,protect,maintain”,hence eventually a loan translation of from Old French maintenir and/or from Latin manūtenēre. The possible French origin and the earlier attestation of from Middle Dutch hanthaven (1286) and from Middle Low German handhafen (1330) suggest that the word may have been borrowed through these. The Germanic formation must be denominal,which is particularly obvious in the northern languages (where the verb “to have” is ''hebben''),but is also seen in High German from the invariably regular conjugation. The nominal element may be from Middle High German thaft,handle,from Old High German hanthaba,from Old High German anthaba (also from Old Saxon handhava; from Middle Dutch hanthave only attested 1490),but the semantics seem problematic. Alternatively a new compound from ''hant''+from Middle High German habe,from Middle Dutch tpossession,belongings; cf. from Middle High German hanthab (“stolen good”,ca. 1350).|Pronunciation}Ⓓ0/0d/De-handhaben.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#to handle,wield,manipulate}#to manage,control,operate}#obsolete to protect someone; to enforce their rights|Derived terms}Handhabung|See also}hantieren

*Haufen*de{}|Alternative forms}Haufe|Etymology}From a merger of from Middle High German hūfe (from Middle High German hūf),from Middle High German houf (from Middle High German houfe),from Old High German hūfo (more southern) and from Old High German houf (more northern),from Proto-Germanic ⋆hūpô and its ablaut variant from Proto-Germanic ⋆haupaz,respectively. With the former is cognate from Middle Low German hūpe,with the latter from Dutch hoop,from English heap.}Already in Middle High German the two forms began to influence each other such that the originally weak from Middle High German hūfe developed the strong byform from Middle High German hūf,while the originally strong from Middle High German houf developed the weak byform from Middle High German houfe. In Modern Standard German the vowels ''-ū-'' and ''-ou-'' regularly coalesced into ''-au-'',which completed the merger. The strong stem is preserved in zuhauf.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhaʊ̯fən/}De-at-Haufen.ogg(Austria)}Ⓓ9/9a/De-Haufen.ogg}Hau+fen|Noun}(mask.,diminituve:Haufen)}#heap,hive,pile}#crowd,lot,group}#euphemism feces,turd

*Hausaufgabe*de{}|Etymology}[[[Haus]+[t1house,home]]+[Aufgabe]]+[t2task]|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhaʊ̯sʔaʊ̯fˌɡaːbə/}Ⓓ0/08/De-Hausaufgabe.ogg}Haus+auf+ga+be|Noun}(fem.)}#homework assignment,a piece of exercise or examination by which a teacher or examiner tries the performance of a student}#}quote-book:passageDie  Notwendigkeit,Kläger  und  Beklagten,Streitgegenstand  und  Antrag  festzustellen,führt  dazu,daß  der  Bearbeiter  einer  Klausur- oder  '''Hausaufgabe'''  sich  schon  an  dieser  Stelle  gezwungen  sieht,sich das für die weitere Prüfung der Zulässigkeit der Klage  so  wichtige  Begehren  zu  vergegenwärtigen.}#}quote-book:passageOft  setzen  sich  allerdings  hier  Mängel  fort,die während  des  Studiums,insbesondere   in   der   Vorbereitungsphase, falls  es  eine  gegeben   hat, nicht  beseitigt  wurden,was  ein  Blick auf  die hohen  Rückgabeziffern  bei  den  '''Hausaufgaben'''  ebenso  beweist,wie  die gleichfalls  beträchtlichen  Aussteigerquoten  in  den  Klausuren.}#}Hausaufgabe '''Hausaufgaben''' sind in der Verhaltenstherapie unverzichtbar und sind von Therapiebeginn bis -ende indiziert (Callan et al. 2019).}•'''Homework''' cannot be forgone in w:behavioral therapy and is indicated from beginning till end of therapy (Callan et al. 2019).|Usage notes}''The plural '''Hausaufgaben''''' indicates homework in general}In educational context,the terms ''Hausaufgabe'' and Hausarbeit are largely interchangeable in principle. Apart from local preferences,we can distinguish those domestic exercises given in w:compulsory school,those given in further educational institutions,and even those part of vocational examinations.}:For instance,one such assignment,variably named by the either term,was historically part of the state certification program (Staatsprüfung) required after w:finishing law school in Germany to gain access to legal professions,rather than included in school programs,until reformed in that respect by the w:Bologna Process in 2003 (see the https://www.bundesjustizamt.de/DE/Service/Justizstatistiken/Justizstatistiken_node.html#AnkerDokument44060 ministerial statistics for all states following this year),after which,in favour of greater import of scientific study of the law,universities had to examine a final coursework Hausarbeit along a written five-hour test Aufsichtsarbeit according to the w:case method in one w:specialization area,the Schwerpunktbereich,the examinations about which weigh 30 % of the total mark according to federal requirement (https://dejure.org/gesetze/DRiG/5d.html § 5d Abs. 2 w:DRiG). the remaining 70 % left for the state to examine. A limited number of term papers called Hausarbeit and such a final one,if not a thesis – not required for a w:considerable list of state-regulated professions prepared for in science colleges –,remain the only scientific works many German university students have to complete,and homework ''Hausaufgaben'' is no general occurrence after secondary education; ''Hausarbeiten'' is the name of w:scientific works obligatory over the semesters of academic graduation. In comparison to Anglo-Saxon education systems,the Central European nudges towards students are low,see ''w:Bummelstudent'',so Hausaufgabe sounds childish at that stage of education:distinguish Übungsaufgabe,alternatively Wiederholungsaufgabe.

*heben*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German heben,from Middle High German heven (rarer from Middle High German heffen),from Old High German heffen,from Old High German heven,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆habbjan. Compare from Dutch heffen,from English heave,from Danish hæve. from German kapieren.}The ''-b-'' is regular in the past tense and participle. In Middle High German the paradigm was regularised by spreading ''-b-'' to the present tense; reinforced in East Central German by the local shift ''-v-'' → ''-b-'' (as in from East Central German Oben for Ofen). The fricative is preserved in related Hefe. The original past forms hub,gehaben were retained until Early Modern German. The verb was then shifted to the class of fliegen etc. (Compare from Dutch heffen,which was also shifted,though to a different ablaut class.)|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈheːbm̩}Ⓓ1/14/De-heben.ogg}Ⓓ3/39/De-heben2.ogg|Verb}heben(hob:hubarchaic,gehoben,höbe:hübearchaic)}#transitive to lift; to raise}#transitive to heave; to hoist}#reflexive to rise; to lift|Derived terms}abheben}anheben}aufheben}ausheben}beheben}darunterheben}drüberheben}einheben}emporheben}entheben}erheben}Gewichtheben}Hebebühne}Heben}heraufheben}herausheben}herüberheben}herunterheben}hervorheben}hinaufheben}hinausheben}hineinheben}hinüberheben}hinwegheben}hochheben}überheben}überheblich}umheben}unterheben}verheben}wegheben}zurückheben

*Heidi*de{}|Etymology}Originally a Swiss German diminutive of Adelheid+-i|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhaɪ̯di/|Proper noun}Heidi:}#Given Name}#}'''1880''' Johanna Spyri,''Heidi's Lehr- und Wanderjahre. Ein neues Capitel und lauter neue Dinge''),p. 95,translated as ''Heidi'':}#}:„Willst du lieber '''Heidi''' heißen,oder Adelheid?“ fragte Klara. „Ich heiße nur '''Heidi''' und sonst Nichts“,war '''Heidi's''' Antwort. „So will ich dich immer so nennen“,sagte Klara; „der Name gefällt mir für dich,ich habe ihn aber nie gehört,ich habe aber auch nie ein Kind gesehen,das so aussieht wie du.+"Would you rather be called '''Heidi''' or Adelaide?" asked Clara. "I am never called anything but '''Heidi'''," was the child's prompt answer. "Then I shall always call you by that name," said Clara,"it suits you. I have never heard it before,but neither have I ever seen a child like you before.

*heikel*de{}|Etymology}Probably a dialectal variant of from Middle Low German disgusting,from which Cognate German loathing,disgust,fastidiousness. A connection to from Proto-Germanic fearful has been suggested for both words; compare from Old English burdensome,troublesome,from English ache,from Galician to vex,from Dutch terrible.}''Heikel'' seems to have arisen out of 16th century Upper German dialects with a first meaning “easily disgusted,choosy”. Dialectal variants include from Bavarian haglich and from Bavarian hoaglich (both akin to regional from German heikelig or heiklig),from Swabian haikel,from Alemannic German heikχel,from Saterland Frisian fastidious with regard to food.}Others have suggested a derivation from Middle High German heien,from Middle High German to cherish,harbour (compare from Bavarian haigeln). The connection with the root of from Iraqw to irritate,annoy,bother,advanced by the Grimms,seems to be out of question today,even given the Upper German verb erkeln.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈhaɪ̯kəl/}Ⓓ3/39/De-heikel.ogg|Adjective}}#delicate gloss:requiring careful handling}•synononym [[[[[brenzlig],[unangenehm]],[schwierig]],[delikat]],[diffizil]],[riskant]}#Austria picky,choosy}•synononym [[anspruchsvoll],[wählerisch]],[verwöhnt]

Verlag,page 13–14:}#}:Ländlich bodenständige Kinder waren die drei und wurzelten mit allen Herzensfasern in dem Stückchen Erde,das sie '''Heimat''' nannten.+The three of them were rural down-home children and were rooted with all fibres of the heart in the little piece of soil that they called home.}#}Heimat Doch für uns gibt es kein Klagen,/ewig kann nicht Winter sein,/einmal werden wir froh sagen:/'''Heimat''' du bist wieder mein.:translationBut we are not to complain,/winter cannot last forever,/one day we will say with joy:/'''homeland''',you are mine once more.}#figurative home; homeland; place where something originated or where it is deep-rooted}•synononym [Ursprungsland],[Heimatland]}•Bayern ist die '''Heimat''' von Brezeln und Weißbier.}•Bavaria is the '''homeland''' of pretzels and wheat beer.|Usage notes}''Heimat'' is often considered a particularly German concept,because it does not have perfect semantic equivalents in many European languages (including English). ''Heimat'' refers to a place towards which one has a strong feeling of belonging,and (usually) a deep-rooted fondness. Most commonly this is one's native region,but it may also be that where one has lived for long,where one has grown up,where one's family are,or where one feels at home for whatever reason.}''Heimat'' may be the whole of one's native country,but more often it is a relatively narrow region (typically with its particular traditions,landscape,dialect,and so on). Even if it refers to a country,it is always defined exclusively by a person's ''emotional'' ties with it,and is therefore quite different from the French m:patrie.|Derived terms}-top3}terms derived from ''Heimat'' (noun)}beheimaten}beheimatet}Beheimatung}Heimatabend}Heimatadresse}Heimatanschrift}Heimatarmee}heimatberechtigt}Heimatberechtigter}Heimatberechtigung}Heimatbereich}Heimatbewusstsein}Heimatbewußtsein}Heimatbezirk}Heimatboden}Heimatbund}Heimatdichter}Heimatdichterin}Heimatdichtung}Heimatdorf}Heimaterde}Heimatfilm}Heimatflotte}Heimatflughafen}Heimatflugplatz}Heimatforscher}Heimatforscherin}Heimatforschung}Heimatfreund}Heimatfreundin}Heimatfront}heimatgebunden}Heimatgefühl}Heimatgewässer}Heimathafen}Heimatinsel}Heimatklänge}Heimatkrieger}Heimatkriegerin}Heimatkunde}Heimatkundler}Heimatkundlerin}heimatkundlich}Heimatkunst}Heimatland}heimatlich}Heimatliebe}Heimatlied}Heimatliederbuch}Heimatliederschreiber}Heimatliederschreiberin}heimatlos}Heimatlose}Heimatlosenheim}Heimatloser}Heimatlosigkeit}Heimatmarkt}Heimatmuseum}Heimatort}Heimatpflege}Heimatplanet}Heimatprovinz}Heimatrecht}Heimatregion}Heimatroman}Heimatschein}Heimatschlag}Heimatschriftsteller}Heimatschriftstellerin}Heimatschuss}Heimatschuß}Heimatschutz}Heimatschutzministerium}Heimatschutzminister}Heimatschutzministerin}Heimatsgebiet}Heimatshafen}Heimatskriegsgebiet}Heimatsort}Heimatsprache}Heimatstadt}Heimatstaat}Heimatstube}Heimattaubenschlag}Heimattreffen}Heimaturlaub}heimatverbunden}Heimatvertreibung}heimatvertrieben}Heimatvertriebene}Heimatvertriebener}Heimatwelt}Obdach- und Heimatlosenheim}Sozial- und Heimatlosenheim}Urheimat}Wahlheimat}-bottom|See also}Bavarian:Hoamat,(Bavarian)}Silesian:Heemte,(East Central German)

*-heit*de{}|Alternative forms}-keit|Etymology}From Middle High German -heit,from Old High German -heit,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆-haidu,ultimately from Proto-Germanic tpersonality,character,manner,way. Cognate with from Dutch -heid,from English -hood,from Danish -hed.|Pronunciation}IPA:haɪ̯t}The suffix has secondary stress when it follows an unstressed syllable and often also when it precedes one. When it is entirely unstressed,the IPAchar:/h/may be unpronounced in common speech.}Ⓓ4/4f/De--heit.ogg|Suffix}(fem.)}#Converts an adjective into a noun and usually denotes an abstract quality of the adjectival root. It is often equivalent to the English suffixes -ness,-th,-ty,-dom:}•schön}•neu}#Converts concrete nouns into abstract nouns:}•Kind}•Christ|Usage notes}While  is the normal form of this suffix,it becomes -keit after certain adjectival suffixes. These are -bar,-ig,-isch,-lich,-sam. For example:nützlich.}Adjectives ending in unstressed  usually take  as well:eitel,mager. However,there are a handful of exceptions,e.g. Dunkelheit,Sicherheit.}Sometimes -ig is added to the adjective and the suffix thus becomes . This is the general rule with adjectives in -haft and -los:fehlerhaft. There is also a fairly large number of other adjectives that follow this pattern:müde. Two forms may exist for some adjectives,occasionally with a semantic distinction,e.g. Neuheit versus Neuigkeit.|Derived terms}suffixsee:de

Some writers may use the spelling ''henk-'' instead of ''häng-'' because it is suggestive of Henker.}Those forms in which the stem ''henk-'' is not followed by a consonant () are audibly distinct from hängen. *Hermelin*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German hermelīn,from Old High German harmilī,diminutive of from Old High German termine,from Proto-Germanic ⋆harmô. Cognates outside Germanic only in from Latvian sermulis and from Lithuanian šarmuõ,from Lithuanian šermuõ.}The monophthong ''-i-'' in modern German (alongside obsolete Hermlein,Hermelein) as well as the final stress can be explained natively,as being from a non-diphthongising dialect on the one hand,and by comparing the irregular stress shift in such words as Holunder,Wacholder,lebendig on the other. However,it seems likely that both developments were reinforced by Romance words such as from Italian ermellino,it,from French hermine. The origin of these latter is contested; they are either borrowed from Germanic or go back to an unrelated litArmenian mouse.|Pronunciation}IPA:/hɛʁməˈliːn/}Ⓓ8/8d/De-Hermelin.ogg|Noun}(neut.)}#zoology ermine (taxfmt:species)}#heraldry ermine|Noun}(mask.)}#ermine gloss:white fur of the ermine}#A moth (taxlink:species (taxfmt:family spp.))}•synononym gelber Hermelin

*Herz*de{}|Alternative forms}Herze|Etymology}From Middle High German herze,from Old High German herza,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hertā,from Proto-Germanic heart,from Proto-Indo-European heart.}Cognate with from Dutch hart,from English heart,from Danish hjerte,from Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍄𐍉.|Pronunciation}IPA:hɛɐ̯t͡s}De-Herz.ogg(Germany)}De-at-Herz.ogg(Austria)}Hertz|Noun}(neut.,plural:[Herzensesvery rare.weak.daten],diminituve:Herz)}#heart}#card games hearts}#sweetheart,darling|Usage notes}'''''Herz''''' has irregular singular declension and is the only noun of its kind.}:}The '''genitive''' singular takes the ending '''''-ens''''':''des Herzens''. The form ''des Herzes'' is less common and only used in medicine.}:}The '''dative''' singular traditionally takes '''''-en''''':''dem Herzen''. This form is still the only accepted standard form in many—more or less fixed—expressions,such as im Herzen,von Herzen,zu Herzen,''Operation'' am offenen Herzen,mit halbem Herzen,and others.

*heulen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German hiulen,from Old High German hūwilōn,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hūilōn.|Pronunciation}IPA:/hɔʏ̯lən/}Ⓓ8/8c/De-heulen.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#to howl,to whine gloss:make a loud,usually high-pitched sound}#sometimes to weep,to cry see usage notes}•synononym weinen|Usage notes}Both in colloquial and literary German,''heulen'' often has a deprecatory tone,implying that the weeping is unjustified and exaggerated. However,in the vernacular it is also commonly used as an entirely neutral synonym of weinen. So one could say in an affectionate and consoling manner:''Ach Schatz... jetzt heul doch nicht! Komm her zu mir!'' (“Oh honey... now don’t cry! Come to me!”). In literary German,''heulen'' is used neutrally only for very intense or desperate weeping,especially referring to small children.|Derived terms}heulen wie ein Schlosshund}mit den Wölfen heulen}zum Heulen sein}man muss mit den Wölfen heulen

In European popular belief,they represent a gateway to the world of fairies or witches,a parallel universe with its own laws and time dimensions. The rings testify to dark forces:demons,falling stars,lightning strikes. It is bad luck to jump into such a ring.
